recipe.definition: The instructions for making one item: which materials it consumes, what it produces, and any workbench or skill level required. The Crafting page shows what you have against what a recipe needs.

drone.definition: An uncrewed machine that carries out a job on its own. A mining drone in HumanityOS flies to one asteroid at a time, fills its hold, and comes back, so the haul is limited by what it can carry.

simulation.definition: The 3D world inside HumanityOS where you practice growing, building, and powering a home. Mistakes there cost nothing, and the skills are meant to carry straight into real life.

fps.definition: How many complete images the game draws each second. Higher feels smoother, 60 is comfortable, and every graphics setting that adds detail costs some of it.

vsync.definition: A setting that hands each finished frame to the monitor in step with its refresh. It removes the torn, split-looking image you otherwise get during fast motion, at the cost of capping the frame rate.

field_of_view.definition: How wide an angle the camera takes in, measured in degrees. Higher shows more around you with a mild stretch at the edges, lower feels zoomed in.

render_distance.definition: How far away, in meters, objects are still drawn. Raising it shows more of the world and makes the graphics card work harder.

ambient_occlusion.definition: Shading that darkens crevices and the places where surfaces meet, because less light reaches into them. It is a cheap way to make objects look planted rather than floating.

god_rays.definition: Visible shafts of light where sunlight streams past clouds or terrain edges. The effect is real: it is sunlight scattering off dust and moisture in the air.

procedural.definition: Building content from rules and maths as it is needed instead of drawing and storing it in advance. It is how a whole planet's continents, clouds, and terrain fit into a small download.

raymarching.definition: A rendering method that steps a ray forward through a volume, sampling as it goes, rather than stopping at a solid surface. It is how the game draws clouds with real three-dimensional shape, and it is expensive.

wireframe.definition: A view that draws only the edges of the shapes an object is made from, so you can see its structure. It is a building and debugging aid, not how the world normally looks.

gizmo.definition: An on-screen handle you drag to move, rotate, or resize something. In the construction editor the gizmos are the glowing grips on walls, doors, and windows.

yaw.definition: Turning left or right around the vertical axis, like shaking your head no. It is one of the three ways a camera or craft can rotate.

pitch.definition: Tilting up or down, like nodding your head yes. It is one of the three ways a camera or craft can rotate.

roll.definition: Tipping sideways around the direction you are facing, like an aircraft banking into a turn. It is the third of the three rotation axes.

graph.definition: A structure made of points, called nodes, and the links between them, called edges. Roads, rails, and pipe runs in HumanityOS are built this way: you drop nodes, then wire edges between them.

gpu.definition: The chip that draws the picture on your screen. Nearly every graphics setting trades GPU work for detail, which is why turning things down raises your frame rate.

cpu.definition: The chip that runs the program itself: the simulation, the physics, and the loading of the world. A setting described as costing CPU will not be helped by a better graphics card.

texture.definition: An image wrapped onto a 3D surface to give it color and detail, like wallpaper on a shape. Sharper textures look better close up and take more graphics memory.

particle.definition: One of the many tiny images a game draws in bulk to make rain, snow, smoke, or sparks. Each is cheap on its own but there can be hundreds of thousands at once, so the weather settings cap how many may exist.

respawn.definition: Coming back into the world after your character dies, at a fixed safe spot rather than where you fell. In HumanityOS you wake in the respawner with nothing lost, and press Respawn on the death screen to continue.

stack_size.definition: How many of one item fit in a single inventory slot before a second slot is needed. It is listed on every item's detail panel, and a stack size of 1 means the item never stacks.

durability.definition: How much wear an item can take before it breaks, counted down as you use it. The inventory panel only shows the figure for items that can wear out at all.

resolution.definition: The number of pixels in an image, written as width by height, such as 1920x1080. Higher is sharper and costs more work to draw, plus more data to send when broadcasting.

encoder.definition: The part that squeezes raw video down into a much smaller stream before it is sent. When it cannot keep up it skips ahead rather than falling behind, which is what a dropped-frame count is telling you.

post_quantum.definition: Encryption and signatures designed to stay safe against a future quantum computer, which would break much of what protects the internet today. HumanityOS identities and private messages already use post-quantum algorithms.

dilithium.definition: The signature algorithm HumanityOS uses to prove a message really came from you. It is a published post-quantum standard, and your Dilithium public key is your identity in the app.

kyber.definition: The algorithm HumanityOS uses to agree a secret key with someone so a private message can be encrypted for them alone. It is a published post-quantum standard, and your key is derived from your seed phrase.

e2ee.definition: Scrambling a message on the sender's device so that only the recipient's device can unscramble it. Every server along the way stores unreadable text, so no operator can read your private messages.

zero_knowledge.definition: A design where the service does its job without ever learning what your data says. The HumanityOS relay carries private messages it cannot read, which also means nobody, operator included, can recover them if you lose your key.

did.definition: A name for a person or agent derived from their own key instead of issued by a company. In HumanityOS it looks like did:hum: followed by 22 characters, and no authority can revoke or reassign it.

verifiable_credential.definition: A signed statement one identity makes about another, such as confirming a skill or a completed course. Anyone can check the signature, the issuer can revoke it, and the subject can withdraw it.

revocation.definition: Cancelling something you previously issued, such as a credential or a permission, so it stops counting. Only the identity that issued a credential can revoke it.

base58.definition: A way of writing binary data with letters and digits, leaving out the characters people confuse (zero, capital O, capital I, lowercase l). Identifiers such as did:hum: addresses use it so they survive being copied by hand.

base64.definition: A way of writing binary data as ordinary text so it can be pasted into a message or a file. Group invite tickets are long base64 strings for exactly this reason.

passphrase.definition: A password, usually several words long, that encrypts your identity on this device. Nobody can reset it: if you forget it you restore your identity from your 24-word seed phrase instead.

vault.definition: The encrypted file on your device that holds your identity key. It stays locked until you enter your passphrase, and while it is locked you cannot sign in, send private messages, or trade.

keychain.definition: The secret store built into your operating system (Windows Credential Manager, macOS Keychain, Linux Secret Service). HumanityOS can optionally keep your key there so the app unlocks without typing a passphrase every launch.

plaintext.definition: Text that has not been encrypted, readable by anyone who handles it along the way. HumanityOS warns you before sending a private message as plaintext, which only happens when the recipient's encryption key is not available.

mainnet.definition: The live blockchain network, where tokens hold real value and transactions are permanent. Anything you do there costs real money.

testnet.definition: Practice copies of a blockchain network where the tokens are free and worthless. Solana runs two of them, Devnet and Testnet, so you can try things without risking anything.

blockchain.definition: A shared record of transactions that thousands of computers each keep a copy of, added to in batches called blocks and impossible to quietly rewrite. Solana is the blockchain HumanityOS uses for optional payments; nothing else in the app depends on one.

token.definition: A unit of value issued on top of a blockchain rather than being the network's own coin. On Solana, SOL is the coin and everything else, such as USDC, is a token.

stablecoin.definition: A token deliberately held at a steady value, usually one US dollar, instead of rising and falling like most cryptocurrencies. It is what people use to hold value on a blockchain without riding the price swings.

swap.definition: Trading one token straight for another from your own wallet, with no company holding your money in between. The price can move slightly between pressing the button and the trade completing, which is what slippage tolerance allows for.

smart_contract.definition: A program stored on a blockchain that runs exactly as written whenever someone calls it, with no company in the middle. Swapping tokens and staking work by calling one.

proof_of_stake.definition: The method a blockchain uses to decide who adds the next block: computers put their own coins up as a deposit and lose them if they cheat. It replaces the electricity-hungry mining that older chains use.

ciphertext.definition: A message after encryption: unreadable to anyone without the key. Your private messages reach the server only as ciphertext, which is why whoever runs it cannot read them.

forward_secrecy.definition: A design where getting hold of today's key does not unlock yesterday's messages, because each stretch of conversation uses a fresh one. A private HumanityOS group issues a new key each time someone joins, so newcomers read from that moment on but not before; groups set to shared history keep one key instead, and give that protection up.

hexadecimal.definition: Counting in sixteens, using 0 to 9 and then a to f, which is a compact way to write raw computer data. Keys are usually shown as hex, which is why an identity looks like a long run of digits and letters.

unlock_pin.definition: A short number, 4 to 12 digits here, used instead of your full passphrase on one device you trust. HumanityOS keeps a random device secret in the operating system's keychain and your PIN unlocks it, so someone who steals only one of the two gets nothing.
